Beowulf. The oldest major work of English literature, an Old English epic composed in the eighth century and surviving in a single manuscript. It tells of the warrior Beowulf's three great battles: against the monster Grendel and Grendel's mother and finally a dragon guarding treasure. The poem blends Germanic heroic tradition and pagan mythology and Christian morality, exploring heroism and fate and mortality and the passage from youth to age.

Composed in Old English, or Anglo-Saxon, around seven hundred CE, the poem is preserved in a single manuscript called the Nowell Codex that barely survived a fire in seventeen thirty-one. It consists of thirty-one hundred eighty-two lines in alliterative verse, not rhymed. The hero Beowulf is a Geat warrior from what is now Sweden who comes to Denmark to aid King Hrothgar, whose mead-hall Heorot is plagued by Grendel, a monster terrorizing the court. Beowulf defeats Grendel bare-handed, ripping off the monster's arm. Then he hunts Grendel's mother to her underwater lair and slays her with a giant's sword, descending into the supernatural underworld.

The poem's final movement shifts tone. Beowulf, now king for fifty years, must face a dragon hoarding ancient treasure. His victory comes at the cost of his own life, a darkening vision of heroism. Themes shift across the three sections: youthful prowess and triumph in the Grendel section, the moral ambiguity of revenge and hunting evil into dark places in the Grendel's mother section, and the approach of death and the fragility of human glory in the dragon section.

The poem mingles pagan fatalism, the concept of wyrd or fate, with Christian theology. Beowulf's victories are attributed both to strength and to God's will. Death is inescapable but glorious. Literary influence is immense. Tolkien, a Beowulf scholar, drew on it for The Lord of the Rings. It established the template for heroic fantasy and epic quests and battles with monsters. Seamus Heaney's nineteen ninety-nine translation brought Beowulf to contemporary readers with musical precision and accessibility. Old English is the language of Beowulf and is foundational to English linguistic and literary history. Beowulf is the English epic and the apex of surviving Anglo-Saxon verse. Nearly all other Old English literature is fragmentary or lost. The poem is the central concern of literary study of what constitutes heroic virtue and how it is tested and how it endures beyond death in reputation.
